Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end). The NCCN/ESMO flowcharts from the slides are kept as pictures under each topic.

Incidence & risk factors

  • Globally > 1,000,000 cases/year.
  • Fifth most frequently diagnosed cancer; third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the world.
  • Less common than colorectal cancer locally; higher incidence in some Eastern populations (e.g. Korea). More common in males.
  • Risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, diet, age, M >> F, family history, previous gastric surgery.
  • Doctor's full list: increasing age, male sex, family history/genetic predisposition, smoking, H. pylori, salt-preserved foods, smoked/processed meats (e.g. hot dogs), sugary drinks, alcohol, previous gastric surgery (esp. prior peptic ulcer resection). Dietary factors = correlation/risk, not necessarily direct causation.
  • H. pylori (prevalence ~25–30% in the lecture) disrupts mucosal protection → ulceration/chronic gastritis → persistent inflammation → impaired repair + accumulation of mutations → cancer.
Long-standing repetitive inflammation → increased malignancy risk.
  • Organism that carries the risk of upper GI neoplastic disease → Helicobacter pylori (commonest cause of peptic ulcer and gastric adenocarcinoma worldwide). 431 ×3
  • MALToma with evidence of H. pylori → treatment antibiotics (H. pylori eradication — low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma regresses after eradication). 434

Hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes

  • 3–5% of all gastric cancers are inherited cancer predisposition syndromes (notes: ~5%) → referral to a cancer genetics professional is recommended.

Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (HDGC)

The most important inherited gastric cancer syndrome — know this. Autosomal dominant; germline truncating mutations in the tumour-suppressor gene CDH1 (encodes E-cadherin, a cell-adhesion protein) — found in 30–50% of HDGC families → diffuse-type gastric cancer.
  • Prophylactic total gastrectomy (without D2) recommended between 18 and 40 years.
  • Screening endoscopy with multiple random biopsies every 6–12 months when prophylactic gastrectomy is not performed.
  • Women have increased risk of breast cancer (lobular).
  • Lifetime gastric cancer risk is very high — almost 100%. Carriers may be offered prophylactic total gastrectomy from young adulthood (~18) or need extensive lifelong surveillance. Once a mutation is found → offer relatives genetic testing/counselling.

  • Others: ataxia-telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, hereditary breast & ovarian cancer syndrome, Li-Fraumeni, Cowden syndrome.
  • Lecture focus for examination/management = HDGC/CDH1.

Classifications

  • Lauren: intestinal, diffuse, mixed. WHO: papillary, tubular, mucinous, poorly cohesive, signet ring. Borrmann (advanced GC): polypoid, fungating, ulcerative, diffusely infiltrating.
Lauren typeKey association (doctor)
IntestinalLynch syndrome
DiffuseHDGC / CDH1
MixedFeatures of both

Linitis plastica

  • Macroscopic thickening of the gastric wall, often the entire stomach; no distinct mass; submucosal infiltration; poorly distensible stomach.
  • Difficult to obtain tissue diagnosis. Treatment: total gastrectomy and lymphadenectomy. Aggressive biology (peritoneal mets).
  • Diffuse infiltrative form: the stomach does not inflate normally with air at endoscopy; superficial mucosal biopsy may be false-negative (tumour is deep/submucosal).
Suspected linitis plastica → EUS-guided biopsy (targets the deep layers) or tunnel biopsy (repeated biopsies at the same site to reach the submucosa).

Presentation

  • Early disease can be asymptomatic.
  • Symptoms: indigestion, nausea and vomiting, dysphagia, postprandial fullness, loss of appetite, melena, haematemesis, weight loss.
  • Late complications: peritoneal/pleural effusions, gastric outlet obstruction, bleeding, jaundice, cachexia.
  • The stomach has a large capacity → body tumours can grow large before symptoms; tumours at narrow regions (GEJ, pylorus) cause symptoms earlier.
Late findingSignificance
ObstructionDistension, vomiting; succussion splash with gastric outlet obstruction
BleedingAnaemia or overt GI bleeding
PerforationSurgical emergency
Virchow nodeLeft supraclavicular lymphadenopathy — metastatic spread
Sister Mary Joseph nodulePeriumbilical metastatic deposit
Alarm features → endoscopy: dysphagia · weight loss · significant anaemia · symptoms failing to respond to treatment.
  • 69-year-old, vague epigastric pain for 2 months + 15 kg weight loss, normal exam, US and CT → next step upper GI endoscopy. 437 ×5
  • 68-year-old, recurrent non-bilious vomiting of undigested food, 13 kg weight loss, cachectic and pale → obstructed gastric outlet (from gastric cancer). 439 ×2

Work-up & staging

  • History and examination; CBC and comprehensive chemistry profile.
  • Upper GI endoscopy and biopsy (include the Siewert type if EGJ adenocarcinoma).
  • EUS; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; FDG-PET/CT if clinically indicated; diagnostic laparoscopy.
  • Labs: CBC, LFTs, renal function, nutritional profile. Endoscopy report should describe the location and relation to the GEJ.
There is no specific tumour marker that reliably diagnoses gastric cancer.
  • Antral adenocarcinoma consented for surgery — the low blood level that suggests nutritional deficiency → albumin. 430 ×2
  • Siewert I, II, III — GEJ tumour mainly on the oesophageal side, at the junction, or on the gastric side.

EUS

  • Essential for small/early lesions (T1 and T2). Endoscopic resection is needed to differentiate T1a vs T1b.
  • Operator dependent; T-stage accuracy 60–90%, N-stage accuracy 50–80%.
  • EUS defines depth (T stage) by seeing the individual wall layers — most useful to separate early T1 from T2. If CT already shows clearly advanced transmural disease, EUS adds little.

Diagnostic laparoscopy

  • Indicated for ≥ T1b; cytology of peritoneal fluid; done prior to chemotherapy and for patients undergoing R0 resection or chemoradiation; can avoid unnecessary laparotomy.
  • The peritoneum is a major metastatic site; small deposits are missed on CT. At laparoscopy: inspect for deposits → if none, peritoneal lavage (saline in the quadrants → aspirate → cytology).
  • Cytology takes time → staging laparoscopy is done as a separate staging procedure, not followed straight away by gastrectomy.
T1b (submucosal invasion) or deeper → significant risk of occult peritoneal metastasis → staging laparoscopy.
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma on biopsy → most appropriate next step → CT scan (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; EUS/laparoscopy follow). 433

AJCC TNM and clinical stage groups (cTNM)

  • Overall approach: symptoms/alarm features → history, exam, labs → endoscopy + biopsy → CT-CAP + EUS ± diagnostic laparoscopy/peritoneal cytology → TNM → treat by stage.

Treatment

  • Multidisciplinary tumour board; combined modality therapy: surgery, chemotherapy, chemoradiation, targeted therapies.

Total vs subtotal gastrectomy

Total gastrectomy (D1/D2 nodal stations) with Roux-en-Y reconstruction

Subtotal (distal) gastrectomy

  • Proximal tumour → total gastrectomy; distal tumour → subtotal/distal gastrectomy, both usually with D2 lymphadenectomy; reconstruction commonly Roux-en-Y.

Regional lymphatics

  • Resection should include perigastric nodes (D1) and those along the named vessels of the coeliac axis (D2) — goal: examine ≥ 16 lymph nodes.
  • D1 = gastrectomy + resection of the greater and lesser omenta (right and left cardiac, lesser and greater curvature, suprapyloric along the right gastric artery, infrapyloric nodes).
  • D2 = D1 + nodes along the left gastric, common hepatic, coeliac and splenic arteries.
  • D1 = perigastric stations 1–7; D2 = second-order nodes along branches of the coeliac trunk. Standard oncological gastrectomy = gastrectomy + D2.

Classifying patients

  • Localized (cTis or cT1a) · Locoregional (cT1b–cT4a; cM0) · Metastatic (cT4b; cM1).
  • By fitness/resectability: medically fit + potentially resectable; medically fit + unresectable; non-surgical candidates.
Unresectable: peritoneal involvement (including positive cytology), distant metastases, locally advanced disease (N3/N4 nodes, invasion of major vascular structures excluding splenic vessels).

East vs West guidelines

Guideline logos on the slides (NCCN, ESMO, Japanese Gastric Cancer Association) (18)

Early gastric cancer

  • T1 lesion regardless of nodal status; uncommon, often incidental.
  • T1a (mucosa) ~5% LN mets; T1b (submucosa) ~15–20% LN mets.
EMR/ESD criteria: well/moderately differentiated · non-ulcerated · T1a (mucosa) · ≤ 2 cm.
Stage (doctor)Approach
Tis / T1a (very early, < 2 cm, no mets)Endoscopic resection
T1bSurgical resection (not endoscopic)
T2 or higherNeoadjuvant chemo → surgery → adjuvant chemo
  • Exact chemotherapy protocols were not required — know the modality and sequence.

Locoregional disease

  • Perioperative chemotherapy for all non-metastatic ≥ cT2 or ≥ N1.
  • D2 lymph node dissection recommended for all ≥ cT2 or ≥ N1 (NCCN recommends but doesn't require it as long as > 15 LNs are examined).
  • Chemoradiation is recommended for patients who received less than a D2 dissection.
  • Radiotherapy is not routine after adequate surgery — mainly for positive margins or an inadequate lymph node harvest (< 15–16 nodes). Otherwise → adjuvant chemotherapy.

  • MAGIC first showed the survival benefit of perioperative chemotherapy (chemo → surgery → chemo) — gold standard until FLOT4 (OS 50 vs 35 months).
  • FLOT = docetaxel/oxaliplatin/leucovorin/fluorouracil.

The operation, step by step

1. Take down the gastrocolic omentum (get into the lesser sac) · 2. High ligation of the left gastro-epiploic

3. High ligation of the right gastro-epiploic · 4. Transect the duodenum

5. High ligation of the right gastric · 6. High ligation of the coronary vein

7. High ligation of the left gastric · 8. Proximal gastric transection

Margin

  • NCCN ~4 cm (updated to R0); ESMO 5 cm (8 cm for diffuse).
  • Consider frozen section when additional margin can be obtained without significant morbidity.

NCCN — postoperative management by R0/R1/R2 resection and pT/N stage (R1/R2 → chemoradiation)

Follow-up & recurrence

Unresectable, metastatic & complicated disease

NCCN — unresectable disease

  • Most metastatic gastric cancers → palliative treatment. Extensive metastasectomy for solid-organ mets is not standard; peritoneal metastases also imply palliative disease. HIPEC is offered in selected centres but is not standard.
  • Adjacent organ involvement: pre-op (perioperative) chemotherapy → diagnostic laparoscopy → en-bloc resection.
  • Obstructed: decompress (NGT) → stage → tumour board → surgery if M0 — start with diagnostic laparoscopy to avoid an unnecessary laparotomy.
  • In M1 patients fit for surgery with reasonable prognosis, diverting gastrojejunostomy is preferred over stenting (fewer recurrent symptoms).
  • GOO: NG decompression → correct fluids/electrolytes and resuscitate → complete staging → if the obstruction prevents neoadjuvant chemo, consider upfront surgery then chemotherapy.

Summary

  • Often diagnosed at advanced stages.
  • Risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, high salt intake.
  • Some cancers are associated with inherited predisposition syndromes.
  • Multidisciplinary team management is essential.
  • Best supportive care is integral, especially in locally advanced or metastatic disease.

  • GIST cell of origin → interstitial cells of Cajal (GI pacemaker cells). 435
  • 6-cm GIST, no metastasis → surgical resection with negative margins (the source's version marks wedge resection — GISTs need clear margins, no lymphadenectomy, since lymphatic spread is uncommon). 442 ×2
  • Epigastric pain, calcified mass, high 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) → carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumour. 434 ×2

Gastric Carcinoma
1. Epidemiology
  • 26,000 new cases annually in the U.S.
  • Incidence has dropped by two-thirds in the last 40 years (due to declining H.

pylori infection).

  • High-risk regions: South Korea (41.8 per 100,000).
  • More common in men (2:1 ratio) and in patients aged 40–60 (mean age 63).
Risk Factors
  • H. pylori infection (3.6- to 18-fold increased risk).
  • Chronic atrophic gastritis (precursor to cancer).
  • Dietary factors (low vegetable/fruit intake, high salt, starch, smoked foods).
  • Smoking.
2. Pathology & Classification
Histology
  • 95% of gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas.
  • Two major histologic types:
  • Intestinal type → Better prognosis, glandular differentiation.
  • Diffuse type → Poorly differentiated, infiltrative, worse prognosis.
  • Signet ring cell carcinoma → More common in younger patients and women.
Morphologic Types

1. Ulcerating carcinoma (25%) → Deep, penetrates all layers.

2. Polypoid carcinoma (25%) → Large, bulky, late metastasis.

3. Superficial spreading carcinoma (15%) → Limited to mucosa/submucosa,

  • best prognosis.

4. Linitis plastica (10%) → Infiltrative growth, rigid stomach, poor prognosis.

5. Advanced carcinoma (35%) → Large tumors extending beyond stomach.

Common Locations:
  • Antrum (40%).
  • Body/Fundus (30%).
  • Cardia (25%).
  • Entire stomach (5%).
Spread:
  • Direct invasion → Pancreas, liver, colon.
  • Lymphatic metastases.
  • Peritoneal dissemination → Krukenberg tumors (ovary), Blumer shelf (rectum).
  • Virchow node (left supraclavicular lymph node).

Staging is crucial (Table 25-3 outlines TNM staging).

3. Clinical Presentation
Early symptoms are non-specific:
  • Postprandial fullness.
  • Mild dyspepsia.
  • Anorexia (especially for meat).
  • Weight loss (most common, ~6 kg).
Advanced symptoms:
  • Epigastric mass (~25% cases).
  • GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis, occult blood).
  • Obstruction (vomiting, dysphagia if cardia is involved).
  • Signs of metastasis:
  • Virchow node (supraclavicular).
  • Blumer shelf (rectal peritoneal deposits).
  • Krukenberg tumors (ovarian involvement).
4. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Findings
  • Iron deficiency anemia (40%).
  • Elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (65%) → May indicate metastases.
  • HER2 overexpression testing → Guides therapy.
B. Imaging
  • Upper endoscopy with biopsy (Gold Standard) → At least 6 biopsies needed.
  • CT/PET/MRI for staging & metastasis detection.
  • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) → Determines depth of invasion & lymph node

involvement.

  • Laparoscopy → Used in cases where metastases are suspected but not

confirmed on imaging.

C. Barium X-ray (rarely used)
  • Can detect gastric ulcers and mass lesions but false negatives in 20% of cases.
5. Treatment
  • Surgical resection is the only curative option.
  • Preoperative chemotherapy (neoadjuvant) recommended for locally

advanced cases.

A. Surgical Options
1. Distal gastrectomy (For tumors in the antrum)
  • Removes tumor, omentum, duodenum, regional lymph nodes.
  • Reconstruction: Billroth I or II (Roux-en-Y is preferred).
2. Total gastrectomy (For proximal tumors/linitis plastica)
  • Requires splenectomy & Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy.
  • Frozen section at margins to ensure complete resection.
Palliative Surgery:
  • Used for unresectable tumors causing obstruction.
  • Gastrojejunostomy may be done instead of resection.
6. Chemotherapy & Targeted Therapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy:
  • FLOT regimen (5-FU, Leucovorin, Oxaliplatin, Docetaxel).
  • Improves survival and reduces tumor size before surgery.
Adjuvant chemotherapy:
  • Used post-surgery for node-positive disease.
Targeted Therapy:
  • Trastuzumab (HER2-positive tumors).
  • Pembrolizumab (PD-L1 inhibitors for advanced disease).

Palliative chemotherapy for metastatic disease improves survival but is not curative.

7. Prognosis & Survival Rates
  • 5-year survival (U.S.): ~31%.
  • Early gastric cancer (confined to mucosa/submucosa): 90% survival.
  • Advanced gastric cancer (lymph node/metastasis present): <20% survival.
  • In Japan (due to screening programs), early gastric cancer survival is much

higher (~70%).

Death usually results from:
  • Tumor metastasis to liver, lungs, brain, bones.
  • Gastric obstruction leading to malnutrition.
Gastric Leiomyomas & Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs)
1. Overview

Leiomyomas: Benign submucosal growths, usually asymptomatic, may cause bleeding.

Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs):

  • Previously classified as leiomyosarcomas.
  • Arise from interstitial cells of Cajal (pacemaker cells of the GI tract).
  • Most common mesenchymal tumors of the GI tract.
  • Can be malignant depending on size & mitotic index.
  • Locations: Most frequently in the proximal stomach, but also found in intestines, gallbladder, urinary bladder.
2. Clinical Presentation

Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally.

When symptomatic:

  • GI bleeding (occult or overt).
  • Epigastric pain.
  • Early satiety or bloating due to mass effect.
  • Weight loss (if malignant).
  • Perforation (rare) → Severe pain & peritonitis.
Spread:
  • Direct invasion or hematogenous spread (common sites: liver, peritoneum,

omentum).

  • Lymphatic spread is uncommon (unlike adenocarcinomas).
3. Diagnosis
  • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) + fine-needle aspiration (FNA) (higher diagnostic

yield than endoscopic biopsy).

  • CT scan or MRI → Determines tumor size, local invasion, metastases.
  • Immunohistochemistry:
  • c-KIT (CD117) → Key diagnostic marker (95% of GISTs).
  • DOG-1, PDGFRA mutations.
Prognostic factors:
  • Tumor size (>5 cm = high risk).
  • Mitotic index (>10 mitoses per high-power field = high risk).
  • Tumor location (GISTs outside stomach tend to be more aggressive).
4. Treatment
  • GISTs ≥2 cm: Resection is recommended (even if asymptomatic).
  • Small (<2 cm), asymptomatic gastric GISTs:
  • Can be observed with periodic imaging.

✔ Leiomyomas: No intervention unless symptomatic.

A. Surgical Management
  • Wedge or segmental resection (without wide margins, unlike

adenocarcinomas).

  • More extensive resections if metastatic disease (peritoneum, liver).
  • Lymph node dissection NOT required (low risk of lymphatic spread).
B. Targeted Therapy
  • c-KIT and PDGFRA mutations → Respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
  • Imatinib (Gleevec):
  • Used for unresectable, metastatic, or high-risk tumors.
  • Given as neoadjuvant therapy to shrink tumors before surgery.
  • Adjuvant therapy after surgery for high-risk tumors (reduces recurrence).
  • Sunitinib: Second-line for imatinib-resistant GISTs.
5. Prognosis & Follow-up
  • Good prognosis if localized and resected.
  • Poor prognosis if large (>10 cm) or high mitotic index.
  • Follow-up imaging required (to detect recurrence/metastasis).
Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome
1. Overview
  • Also called Wilkie's Syndrome.
  • Rare cause of duodenal obstruction due to compression of the third portion

of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and the aorta.

  • Commonly associated with rapid weight loss → loss of mesenteric fat reduces

the aortomesenteric angle, leading to duodenal entrapment.

  • At-risk populations:
  • Patients with severe burns, trauma, or prolonged immobilization (e.g., body

casts).

  • Anorexia nervosa or malnutrition.
  • Patients undergoing bariatric surgery or experiencing chronic weight loss.
  • Spinal cord injuries or congenital conditions with abnormal SMA anatomy.
2. Pathophysiology
Normal anatomy:
  • SMA leaves the aorta at a 50–60° angle.
  • Aortomesenteric distance = 10–20 mm.
SMA syndrome:
  • Aortomesenteric angle narrows to <25°.
  • Aortomesenteric distance shrinks to <8 mm.
  • Duodenum gets compressed, leading to intermittent or chronic obstruction.
3. Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Postprandial bloating & crampy epigastric pain.
  • Early satiety & weight loss.
  • Nausea & vomiting (bilious, non-bloody).
  • Symptoms improve in the prone or knee-chest position.
  • Malnutrition & electrolyte imbalances in chronic cases.
4. Diagnosis
Imaging Studies:
  • Upper GI series (fluoroscopy):
  • Dilatation of the proximal duodenum.
  • Abrupt "cut-off" at the third portion.
  • Relief in the knee-chest position.
  • CT angiography with contrast:
  • Confirms narrowing of aortomesenteric angle (<25°).
  • Measures reduced aortomesenteric distance (<8 mm).
  • Upper endoscopy: Rules out other causes (e.g., malignancy, peptic ulcer disease).
5. Differential Diagnosis
Scleroderma:
  • Hypomotility & dilated duodenum without significant peristalsis.
  • Usually associated with esophageal dysphagia.
Malrotation with congenital bands:
  • Similar obstruction but congenital in origin.
  • Surgical correction required.
6. Treatment
A. Conservative Management (First-Line)

Indications: Mild to moderate symptoms without severe malnutrition.

Nutritional therapy:

  • High-calorie, small frequent meals.
  • Liquid or enteral feeding (nasogastric/nasoduodenal tube if needed).
  • Parenteral nutrition for severe malnutrition.
  • Postural changes:
  • Prone or left lateral decubitus positioning after meals.
  • Knee-chest position to relieve compression. Fluid & electrolyte management if dehydration is present.
B. Surgical Management (Severe/Refractory Cases)
Indications:
  • Persistent vomiting & weight loss despite conservative treatment.
  • Complete duodenal obstruction.
Surgical options:
  • Strong’s procedure (ligament of Treitz release): Mobilizes the duodenum to

relieve compression.

  • Duodenojejunostomy (bypass procedure): Creates an anastomosis between the duodenum & jejunum.
  • Gastrojejunostomy (less commonly performed).
7. Prognosis & Follow-up
  • Excellent prognosis with early intervention.
  • Most cases improve with nutritional therapy & postural changes.
  • Surgical success rate >90% if needed.
  • Long-term follow-up: Nutritional counseling to prevent recurrence.
